_note: Field Guide content. Stats are read from species.json; this adds real-world facts + strengths/weaknesses + survival tactics. Keep grounded in known paleontology.

velociraptor.facts: Really turkey-sized and feathered, not the movie giant. A nimble pack hunter with a retractable sickle claw on each foot.
weaknesses: Reliant on the pack — scatter it and it falters
velociraptor.survival: Never let them surround you. Put your back to a wall or ruin, use chokepoints, and a flare or loud deterrent breaks the pack.

deinonychus.facts: The dromaeosaur that actually inspired the films' 'raptors'. Hunted in coordinated packs using a killing claw.
deinonychus.survival: Keep your flanks covered and break line of sight between members. Reach the safe zone — they won't follow into the lit perimeter.

troodon.facts: Small, with a large brain and big eyes — one of the keenest-sensed dinosaurs, capable of low-light hunting.
troodon.survival: It hunts by sense — crouch, stay quiet, and keep your noise low. Don't sprint near cover it could be using.

atrociraptor.facts: A short-snouted, sprinter-built dromaeosaur. Built for explosive speed over short distances.
atrociraptor.survival: Don't try to outrun the first burst — break its line and outlast it, then slip to the beacon.

pyroraptor.facts: A feathered raptor; recent finds suggest some dromaeosaurs were comfortable near water.
pyroraptor.survival: Water won't shake it. Use dense cover and ruins to break pursuit.

dilophosaurus.facts: Twin head crests are real — but the venom-spitting frill is pure fiction. The real animal was a slender predator of fish and small prey.
dilophosaurus.survival: It strikes from cover — scan tree lines and ruins. Bright light or a sudden noise will make it think twice.

majungasaurus.facts: A stocky abelisaurid with a short, deep skull and a small head horn. Fossil evidence shows it ate its own kind.
majungasaurus.survival: It can't turn sharply — circle it and cut back. Break the chase and it loses interest.

cryolophosaurus.facts: Found in Antarctica with a distinctive sideways crest above the eyes — nicknamed 'Elvisaurus'.
cryolophosaurus.survival: Keep distance and use terrain — it commits to a straight chase you can break.

monolophosaurus.facts: Named for the single bony crest running along its snout, likely for display.
monolophosaurus.survival: Weave through trees and ruins; don't let it pin you in the open.

ceratosaurus.facts: Sported a blade-like nose horn and a deep, flexible tail — it may have been a capable swimmer.
ceratosaurus.survival: Outrun it in the open and stay out of the water, where it has the edge.

rugops.facts: A lightly-built abelisaurid with weak jaws — most likely a scavenger rather than a big-game killer.
weaknesses: Weak bite, not built for live prey
rugops.survival: Stand your ground with noise and light — it's easily driven off a kill or a cornered survivor.

megalosaurus.facts: The first dinosaur ever scientifically named (1824). A robust, powerful Jurassic predator.
megalosaurus.survival: Juke its turns and break line of sight; don't try to outmuscle it.

allosaurus.facts: An apex Jurassic hunter that attacked with a hatchet-like slashing bite rather than crushing power.
allosaurus.survival: Never trade blows. Keep moving, use cover, and make the beacon — it can't follow inside.

yangchuanosaurus.facts: A large Asian allosauroid — the Jurassic apex of its ecosystem, similar in role to Allosaurus.
yangchuanosaurus.survival: Distance and terrain. Cut around obstacles it must lumber around.

carnotaurus.facts: Bull-horned and built for speed — one of the fastest large predators. Tiny arms and forward-facing eyes for a narrow field of view.
carnotaurus.survival: Bait the charge, then dodge hard sideways at the last second — it can't turn with you. Use its blind flanks.

baryonyx.facts: A fish-eating spinosaurid with a huge thumb claw and croc-like jaws; fossils contain fish scales.
weaknesses: Specialized for fish, less for fast land prey
baryonyx.survival: Stay off the riverbanks — it patrols water's edge. On dry, open ground you have the advantage.

suchomimus.facts: A large spinosaurid with a long crocodilian snout and a low back sail, tied to rivers and lakes.
suchomimus.survival: Avoid the river entirely. It's far less dangerous away from the water.

spinosaurus.facts: The largest known predatory dinosaur — semi-aquatic, with a tall sail and a paddle-like tail. Ruled the rivers.
weaknesses: Most dangerous at the water — less agile on open land
spinosaurus.survival: Never wade or linger by the river. Keep to high, dry ground and it's far easier to evade.

trex.facts: The apex predator. The strongest bite of any land animal, superb smell — and it could absolutely see you standing still (the 'movement vision' is a myth).
trex.survival: Don't rely on staying still. Use cover and elevation, keep noise down, juke its turns, and run for the safe zone.

giganotosaurus.facts: Among the largest land predators ever — slightly longer than T. rex, with a slashing bite and possible pack behavior.
strengths: Enormous and fast for its size
giganotosaurus.survival: Never face it in the open. Weave through ruins and forest to break its line of sight and reach safety.

parasaurolophus.facts: A duck-billed hadrosaur whose long hollow crest worked like a resonating horn for herd communication.
parasaurolophus.survival: Harmless to you. But its blaring alarm calls draw predators — don't spook a herd while hiding nearby.

corythosaurus.facts: A helmet-crested hadrosaur that moved in herds, relying on numbers and vocal alarms.
corythosaurus.survival: Harmless — and useful. A bolting herd is your cue that a predator is near.

iguanodon.facts: A big ornithopod with a sharp conical thumb spike — a genuine defensive weapon. Walked on two legs or four.
iguanodon.survival: Leave it space. Crowd or corner it and the thumb spike will hurt — otherwise it ignores you.

gallimimus.facts: An ostrich-mimic and one of the fastest dinosaurs, with a toothless beak and an omnivorous diet.
gallimimus.survival: Harmless. A sudden stampede of them is a reliable predator alarm — move the opposite way.

dryosaurus.facts: A small, lightly-built, fleet-footed plant-eater that relied on speed and the herd.
dryosaurus.survival: Harmless. Watch which way the herd flees to read where danger is.

hypsilophodon.facts: A small, agile herbivore — once wrongly imagined as a tree-climber; really a fast ground runner.
hypsilophodon.survival: Harmless. Their nervous scattering signals a nearby threat.

triceratops.facts: Three horns and a massive bony frill; among the very last non-bird dinosaurs. Will stand and fight.
triceratops.survival: Don't corner it or approach near young. Keep your distance and it leaves you be — provoke a charge and it's lethal.

pachyrhinosaurus.facts: A ceratopsian with a thick bony pad (boss) over the nose instead of a horn; travelled in big herds.
pachyrhinosaurus.survival: Give the herd room. Unprovoked it ignores you; pressured, the boss is a battering ram.

stegosaurus.facts: Plated back and a spiked tail — the 'thagomizer' — that could impale a predator. Famously tiny-brained.
stegosaurus.survival: Never approach from behind — the tail is deadly. Stay to its front or side and keep your distance.

ankylosaurus.facts: A living tank: armor-plated, with a bony tail club heavy enough to break a predator's bones.
ankylosaurus.survival: Harmless if left alone. Never get near or behind the tail club — keep clear and it won't bother you.

indominus.facts: Not a natural animal. A genetically-engineered apex built from T-Rex, raptor, cuttlefish and tree-frog DNA — intelligent, fast, and able to mask its heat signature. It kills for sport, not food.
strengths: Faster and smarter than a T-Rex
Sets ambushes — remembers where you hid
weaknesses: Arrogant — can be lured and trapped
Rival apexes (T-Rex, Mosasaurus) will fight it
Containment paddocks can still hold it
indominus.survival: You cannot out-fight it. Break line of sight, use the towers and structures, and decide the ending fast — contain it, feed it to the lagoon, or run. Hesitation is death.

mosasaurus.facts: An 17-metre marine reptile that ruled the seas — closer to a monitor lizard than a fish. Ambushes from below and breaches to take prey off the surface.
strengths: Owns the lagoon and river mouth
weaknesses: Bound to water — helpless on land
Slow to re-submerge after a breach
mosasaurus.survival: Stay back from deep water and the river's edge. It can only take what comes within reach of the surface — but anything it grabs is gone.

pteranodon.facts: A large toothless pterosaur with a seven-metre wingspan and a long bony crest. Not a strong flier in still air — it rides thermals and dives on prey.
strengths: Attacks from the air, hard to track
Dives and grabs — can lift a person
weaknesses: Clumsy and vulnerable on the ground
Scattered by flares and loud noise
pteranodon.survival: Get under cover when the flock wheels overhead. Open ground is their kill zone; tree canopy, towers and roofs break their dive.

ultimasaurus.facts: A forbidden four-way chimera — Tyrannosaurus jaws, a Triceratops horned shield, Velociraptor cunning and long grasping arms, and a Kentrosaurus thagomizer. The apex of apexes: no natural predator, and no off-switch.
strengths: Black-horned, spiked frill that shrugs off frontal attacks
Long usable raptor arms that grab and pin
A 360° spiked tail mace that thrashes anything behind it
Relentless — it never breaks off the hunt
weaknesses: Enormous noise signature — it hears you from across the island
Single-minded once locked on; terrain that breaks line of sight buys time
ultimasaurus.survival: Do not fight it. Break contact: put solid ruins or a watchtower between you, cut your noise, and route to extraction. Flares barely faze it — the beacon safe zone is your only reprieve.
